title: WPSS/35/2012 of NAVIN SINGH PANWAR and OTHERS Vs STATE OF UTTARAKHAND and OTHERS

Dated: August 1, 2012
Hon'ble Tarun Agarwala, J.

The petitioners in Writ Petition No.35 of 2012
(S/S) and in Writ Petition No.92 of 2012 (S/S) have
challenged the validity and legality of the
Uttarakhand Absorption on the Posts of Forest
Range Officer Rules, 2011, (hereinafter referred to
as the Absorption Rules of 2011), being arbitrary
and unreasonable and, ultra vires Article 14 and 16
of the Constitution of India. The petitioners are
Deputy Rangers and contend, that by these Rules,
persons working on the post of Assistant
Development Officer (Forest) (hereinafter referred to
as A.D.O.) are being absorbed on a higher post of
Forest Ranger, which post is required to be filled up
by the Public Service Commission.
In order to understand the controversy and
adjudicate the matter between the parties, it is
necessary for the Court to go back in time.
In the Forest Department, there is a hierarchy
of posts, which have been framed under various
Rules, which will be mentioned hereinafter. At the
lowest rung, the lowest post is the post of a Forest
Guard. The service conditions of a Forest Guard is
regulated by the U.P. Lower Subordinate Forest
Service Rules, 1980, in which, it has been indicated

3
that 90% of the posts of Forest Guard would be
filled up by way of direct recruitment and 10% by
way of promotion from Class IV employees. Above
the post of Forest Guard is the post of a Forester.
The service condition of a Forester is governed and
regulated by U.P. Subordinate Forest (Rangers,
Deputy Rangers and Foresters) Service Rules, 1951
(hereinafter referred to as the Rules of 1951). The
post of Forester under these Rules is required to be
filled up by way of promotion from suitable Forest
Guards. The next rung in the ladder is the post of a
Deputy Ranger and under the Rules of 1951, the
post of a Deputy Ranger is required to be filled up
by way of promotion from suitable Foresters. Above
the Deputy Ranger is the post of a Forest Range
Officer. This post is a gazetted Class II post and the
service conditions are governed under the Rules of
1951. However, on 3rd January, 2011, the
Uttarakhand Forest Range Officers Service Rules,
2010 came into existence. Under these Rules, 50%
of the post of Forest Range Officers is required to be
filled up by direct recruitment and the remaining
50% by way of promotion from suitable Deputy
Rangers. Similar Rule was existing in the 1951
Rules. Above the post of a Forest Ranger is the post
of Assistant Conservator of Forest, which belongs to
the State Forest Service. 50% of the post of
Assistant Conservator of Forest is required to be
filled up by promotion from suitable Range Officers
and remaining 50% by direct recruitment.

4

recruitment, the class/category, minimum
educational qualification, pay scale, etc. of a Forest
Guard, Forester, Deputy Ranger and Forest Range
Officer, is indicated hereunder:-

The erstwhile State of U.P. issued a
Government Order dated 10th August, 1976,
creating 52 posts of Junior Forest Ranger for the
plain areas of U.P. This post of Junior Forest
Ranger was an ex-cadre post and was made
equivalent to the post of a Deputy Ranger. By
another Government Order dated 3rd November,
1976, 67 posts of Assistant Development Officer
(Forest) were created for the development of Civil
and Soyem Forest which was sanctioned under the
5th Five Year Plan. These 67 posts were created for
4 Hill Districts, namely, Almora, Pithoragarh, Pauri

5
and Tehri. One Civil and Soyem Forest Division was
sanctioned for each of the four Districts. This post
of A.D.O. was an ex-cadre post and was indicated
to be equivalent to the post of a Deputy Ranger.
Subsequently, executive instructions were issued
by the Government of U.P., indicating that these
posts of Assistant Development Officers would be
filled up by direct recruitment through Rules and
Regulations framed therein, but for reasons best
known, the same was not done. In the case of
appointment of Junior Forest Ranger, an
advertisement was issued in 1976 inviting
applications for 26 posts of Junior Forest Ranger.
In this advertisement, it was indicated that persons
appointed as Junior Forest Ranger would be sent
for training to Northern Forest Ranger's College,
Dehradun for a Rangers Course upon completion of
three years of service as a Junior Forest Ranger.
Based on this advertisement, many people applied
and were appointed as Junior Forest Rangers, but
for reasons best known to the erstwhile State of
U.P. and the Forest Department, the Junior Forest
Rangers were not sent for training to the Institute
for the Rangers Course.
In so far as the appointment of Assistant
Development Officer in the Hill Districts were
concerned, no recruitment process was initiated
nor any service rules or regulations were framed by
the Government, prescribing the minimum
qualification or the mode of selection, recruitment,

6
etc. However, in order to meet the exigencies of
work, options were invited from the Deputy
Rangers, Foresters and even Forest Guards, for
being deputed or being posted as A.D.O. (Forest) in
the Hill Districts. One finds that Deputy Rangers
did not come forward as, in all probability, it was
not remunerative enough for them to be posted in
the Hill Districts since the pay scale of an A.D.O.
was the same as that of a Deputy Ranger, but the
pay scale of a Forester and Forest Guard were lower
and for them it was an attractive offer to be posted
as an A.D.O. The Forest Department sent options
to the Deputy Rangers, Foresters and Forest
Guards to opt for being posted as A.D.O.s and,
upon their options being received, these persons
holding the post of a Deputy Ranger or Forester or
Forest Guard, were posted as A.D.O. In their
posting orders it was stipulated that the post of
A.D.O. is an ex-cadre post and that the persons so
posted will not have any lien on that post. It was
also made clear that future promotion would be
made from their initial cadre on the basis of their
seniority as Deputy Ranger, Forester or Forest
Guard as the case may be. It was also indicated
that the persons so sent as A.D.O. can be reverted
to their original cadre as soon as regular
recruitment to the post of A.D.O. was made. From
time to time, persons holding the post of Forester or
Forest Guard or Deputy Ranger were posted as
A.D.O. and a number of these persons also came

7
back to their original cadre upon their promotion to
the next higher post.
Upon the creation of the State of Uttarakhand,
the Forest Department was reorganized and, by an
order of 6th June, 2005, persons working on the
post of A.D.O. were directed to be reverted back to
their parent department upon completion of 5 years
on the post of A.D.O. Some of these A.D.O.s, being
aggrieved by this reversion order, filed Writ Petition
No.184 of 2006 (S/S), praying not only for the
quashing of the order dated 6th June, 2005, but
also prayed that they should be allowed to function
as A.D.O. and further prayed that the respondents
be directed to consider their eligibility for being
promoted as Forest Ranger against 50% direct
recruitment quota. In this petition, an interim order
was passed, staying the effect and operation of the
order dated 6th June, 2005. As a result of the
interim order, the petitioners continued to work as
A.D.O. and were not reverted to their original cadre.
Apart from the aforesaid, some of the A.D.O.s filed
Writ Petition No.292 of 2003 (S/S) praying that a
cadre be created in the Rules of 1951 for the post of
A.D.O. and that the respondents be directed to
consider the claim of the petitioners for
confirmation on these posts w.e.f. 1st April, 1982. A
further prayer was made that they should be paid
salary in the pay scale of 5500-9000 which is
equivalent to the post of a Deputy Ranger.

8
Some of the petitioners of Writ Petition No.184
of 2006 (S/S) and No.292 of 2003 (S/S) filed
intervention application in Writ Petition No.35 of
2012 (S/S) and No.92/2012 (S/S), which was
allowed and the interveners were impleaded as
necessary respondents and were allowed to file
counter affidavit. Inspite of repeated time being
granted, no counter affidavit has been filed. It was
contended that their stand has been indicated in
the writ petitions filed by them, which may be
considered while hearing Writ Petition No.35 of
2012 (S/S). Accordingly, WPSS No.184 of 2006 and
WPSS No.292 of 2003 were connected and, that is
how all these four petitions are being heard
together.
The contention of the petitioners in WPSS
No.292/2003 is, that they have been working as
A.D.O., which is an ex-cadre post for several years
and no provision has been made with regard to
promotion from the post of A.D.O. and, therefore, a
separate Rule in the Rules of 1951 should be
created and that the petitioners working on these
posts should be confirmed and the pay scale
should accordingly be paid, which is equivalent to
the post of Deputy Ranger.
The contention of the petitioners in WPSS
No.184 of 2006 is that even though they were
initially appointed on the post of a Forester or a
Forest Guard, but subsequently, a fresh
appointment was made on the post of A.D.O. in the

9
year 1995 and 2003 and since then the petitioners
are working on the post of A.D.O. and are drawing
the salary which is equivalent to the pay scale of a
Deputy Ranger. The contention of the petitioners is,
that by the order of 6th June, 2005, the petitioners
were reverted to their original posting as a Forester
and would be given the pay scale of a Forester,
which would not only be unfair but also arbitrary.
The petitioners have contended that the post of
A.D.O. is equivalent to the post of Forest Ranger as
per the Government Order of 3rd November, 1976
and, consequently, they cannot be reverted back to
a lower post. Further, they should also be promoted
as Forest Ranger against 50% direct recruitment
quota.
The contention of the petitioners, in so far as
their claim for promotion to the post of Forest
Ranger is, that in similar situation Junior Forest
Ranger were appointed as Forest Ranger by the
State of U.P. and, in this regard, has placed
reliance upon a decision of the Division Bench of
the Allahabad High Court in the case of Narendra
Kumar Srivastava vs. State of U.P. & Ors.,
decided on 22nd August, 1989 in Writ Petition
No.4817 of 1981 and other connected petition. In
that petition, the case was that pursuant to the
Government Order to create 52 posts of Junior
Forest Ranger for the plain areas, which was
equivalent to the post of Deputy Ranger, the
respondents issued an advertisement dated 11th

10
June, 1976, inviting applications to fill up 26 posts
of Junior Forest Ranger. In this advertisement, it
was indicated that a person so appointed as Junior
Forest Ranger would have to work for 3 years and
thereafter would be sent for training to Northern
Forest Ranger's College, Dehradun for a Rangers
Course and, in due course, would be promoted to
the post of Forest Ranger. Based on the conditions
mentioned in the advertisement, many people
applied and were selected as Junior Forest
Rangers, but for reasons best known, were not sent
for training. Subsequently, in the year 1981, an
advertisement was issued for filling up 70 posts of
Forest Rangers by direct recruitment. Some of the
Junior Forest Rangers filed the writ petition praying
that 45 posts of Forest Rangers should not be filled
up through this direct recruitment/selection
process and that these posts should be utilized to
absorb the Junior Forest Rangers. The writ court,
after considering all aspects of the matter, held that
the State was bound by the principles of
promissory estoppel and that they are bound to
comply with the terms and conditions of the
advertisement of 12th June, 1976. The writ court,
consequently, issued a mandamus to the State
Government to fulfill the conditions of the service
as per the advertisement dated 12th June, 1976,
i.e., to sent those Junior Forest Rangers for
training to the Institution for the Rangers Course
and, if necessary, make necessary amendment in
the existing Rules and, consequently, restrained

11
the State Government from filling 45 posts of Forest
Rangers. The said decision was attacked by the
State Government before the Supreme Court of
India, which was dismissed. It has been stated at
the bar that subsequently the State Government
issued appointment letters to the Junior Forest
Rangers appointing them as Forest Rangers.
In the light of the said decision, the learned
counsel urged that the petitioners are also on the
same footing and are entitled to be promoted as
Forest Rangers and, in the alternative, contended
that their demand for being appointed as A.D.O.
was pending consideration before the State
Government, by which, ultimately the Absorption
Rules of 2011 were issued to absorb the A.D.O.s on
the post of Forest Ranger as a one time process. It
was contended that the Rules of 2011 should be
considered in this light.
The petitioners of WPSS No.35 of 2012 and
No.92 of 2012 contend that these Absorption Rules
of 2011 are arbitrary and violative of Article 14 and
16 of the Constitution of India and are liable to be
quashed. The post of Forest Ranger, being a
gazetted post, comes under the purview of the
Public Service Commission. The appointment on
the post of Forest Ranger has different
qualifications. There is a separate procedure and
there are separate Rules governing the service
conditions of a Forest Ranger and, without going

12
through this criteria, the action of the respondents
in absorbing these Foresters and Forest Guards on
the post of Deputy Ranger, without promoting them
on the post of Deputy Rangers, was wholly illegal
and was also against the provisions of Article 320
of the Constitution of India. It was contended that
by these Absorption Rules of 2011, the Public
Service Commission has been bypassed and the
Principal Chief Conservator of Forest, being the
appointing authority, has been given the power to
absorb these A.D.O.s as Forest Rangers. It was
consequently contended that the absorption can
only be done on the post on which the A.D.O.s were
working or, at the best, on an equivalent post and,
such absorption cannot be done on a higher post,
which has a different pay scale and which has a
different selection process.
The State Government, namely, the Chief
Secretary and the Principal Secretary, respondent
nos.1 and 2, respectively, have tried to justify their
stand, first by raising a plea that the petitioners
have no locus standi as they are not aggrieved
persons. It was contended that these petitioners,
who are Deputy Rangers were eligible to be
promoted as Forest Rangers and, in any case, their
quota of promotion was not being hampered
inasmuch as the absorption under the impugned
Absorption Rules of 2011 was being done from the
quota of direct recruitment. It was further
contended that the Rules so framed for the post of

13
Forest Rangers will not be applicable since Rule 2
of the Absorption Rules of 2011 provides an
overriding effect to any other rules or orders framed
earlier by the State Government. It was also
contended that since it has an overriding effect, the
requirement of the posts, coming under the purview
of the Public Service Commission becomes
immaterial. In this light, the learned Additional
Advocate General has tried to justify the action of
the State Government in issuing the impugned
Absorption Rules of 2011.
The Court finds that respondent no.3 Principal
Chief Conservator of Forest, Uttarakhand, has filed
a separate counter affidavit, contending that the
Absorption Rules are violative of Article 14 and 16
of the Constitution and, are against the existing
Rules of 1951, 2010, Entrance and Training Rules,
2004 and, that the Absorption Rules are not in
conformity with these Rules of 1951 and 2010. The
Principal Chief Conservator of Forest, infact, has
accepted the stand of the petitioners of WPSS No.35
of 2012 and No.92 of 2012.
In the light of the aforesaid, the Court has
heard Sri Rakesh Thapliyal, the learned counsel for
the petitioners in WPSS No.35/2012 and
No.92/2012, Sri Ravi Babulkar, the learned
counsel for the petitioners in WPSS No.184/2006
and Sri Rajendra Dobhal, the learned Senior
Counsel assisted by Sri Mangal Singh Chauhan,
the learned counsel for the petitioners in WPSS

14
No.292/2003 and also on behalf of the A.D.O.s,
who were impleaded in WPSS No.35/2012 and
No.92/2012. The Court has also heard Sri B.D.
Kandpal, the learned counsel for the Public Service
Commission and Sri A.S. Rawat, the learned
Additional Advocate General, who was at a loss of
words in trying to defend the State Government in
view of the counter affidavit filed by the Principal
Chief Conservator of Forest, which the Additional
Advocate General was also representing.
Before we proceed further, attention was
invited to certain provisions, which the Court would
like to address. The Principal Chief Conservator of
Forest in his counter affidavit has submitted that
an opinion was sought from the Forest Department
with regard to the absorption of the A.D.O.s. The
opinion of the Department was conveyed by the
Chief Conservator of Forest by a letter dated 31st
August, 2009 indicating their stand that it would
not be appropriate to frame any scheme for
promotion of A.D.O.s to the post of Forest Ranger
under the prevailing Rules. Again, in response to
the query made by the State Government, the
Forest Department, vide letter dated 31st May,
2010, gave a detailed report bringing on record the
facts as to why it would not be appropriate to frame
any scheme for the A.D.O.s (Forest). The Principal
Chief Conservator of Forest submitted that inspite
of the opinion of the Forest Department, the

15
impugned Absorption Rules of 2011 were framed
under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution.
The Principal Chief Conservator of Forest, in
his counter affidavit, has further submitted that the
Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education
(I.C.F.R.E.) under the administrative control of
Ministry of Environment and Forest, Government of
India, regulates the forestry education and training
of the field staff of Forest Department throughout
the country and that rules/guidelines are issued
from time to time. It was also urged that the
subject "Forest" was included in the concurrent list
of the Constitution and that the Central
Government was also empowered to make
laws/rules on the subject related to forestry under
Article 246(2) of the Constitution. The guidelines
issued by the Central Government from time to
time, being obligatory, was implemented by the
States, namely, that person appointed directly as
Range Forest Officer, must obtain a higher
standard certificate of "Diploma in Forestry" from
the prescribed institute, which is awarded by
Director, Forest Education.
The above mentioned policy/guidelines of
Government of India was subsequently
incorporated in "The Subordinate (Forest Rangers,
Deputy Rangers and Foresters) Service Rules, 1951
enacted by the State of U.P. Rule 5(2) of the Rules
of 1951, which is applicable in the case of direct

16
recruitment to the post of Forest Ranger/Range
Officer, is extracted hereunder:-
"By direct recruitment of candidates who have
been selected through the commission in the manner
prescribed in appendix-A to these rules for
undergoing a course of instruction in the college and
who have obtained the higher standard certificate
after 2 years training therein".
The respondent no.3, in paragraph 23, has
further submitted that in 2004, the Government of
India after consultation with the States, notified a
revised rules pertaining to the entrance and
training of Forest Range Officers called "Entrance
and Training Rules (revised) 2004, for Forest Range
Officers. The Rules of 2004 was published in the
extraordinary Gazette of India on 22nd July, 2004.
In the said Entrance and Training Rules of 2004,
the Government of India made a number of
provisions with respect to the
selection/recruitment/appointment of Range Forest
Officers, some of which are stated below:
i) As per Rule 8, a candidate must possess
Bachelor's Degree (or equivalent) in Science
or Engineering of any recognized university.
ii) Rule 9 prescribes the minimum physical
standard of Height and Chest of the person.
iii) Rule 11 provides for the mode of conducting
a written examination through State Public
Service Commission.

17
iv) Rule 14 provides for the 18 months training
and the prescribed course for it which needs
to be completed successfully by the trainee.
The Principal Chief Conservator of Forest has
further submitted that in conformity with the Rules
of 2004 enacted by the Government of India, the
State of Uttarakhand enacted "The Uttarakhand
Forest Range Officers Service Rules 2010"
regulating the rules of recruitment and the
conditions of service appointed to the Uttarakhand
Forest Range Officers Service. The basic rules of
recruitment as provided in the Rules of 2004 of the
Government of India, being obligatory for the
States, were incorporated in the Service Rules of
2010 enacted by the Government of Uttarakhand.
In other words, the State of Uttarakhand ensured
the compliance of the Rules made by the Central
Government, some which are illustrated below:-
i) In Rule 8, Bachelor's Degree (or equivalent)
in Science or Engineering was prescribed as
the minimum educational qualification. It is
to be informed that in earlier Service Rules
of 1951, the minimum educational
qualification was intermediate science.
ii) In Rule 13, the minimum physical standard
of Height and Chest of the person was
prescribed in the same manner as
prescribed by the Government of India in
rules of 2004.

18
iii) In Rule 5 and 15, the procedure for
conducting a written examination through
State Public Service Commission was also
provided.
iv) Rule 18 provides for the same duration of
training as provided by the Government of
India i.e. of 18 months duration, which was
earlier different.
It has also been brought on record that the
State Government issued an order dated 20th
December, 2006 abolishing ex-cadre post of A.D.O.
(Forest). Further, by this order, it was further
clarified that persons working on the post of A.D.O.
will continue to function as A.D.O. till they retire or
they themselves revert back to their parent
department.
In the light of the aforesaid Government Order
dated 20th December, 2006, the relief claimed by
the petitioners of WPSS No.292 of 2003 cannot be
granted, namely, that a cadre of A.D.O. be created
under the Rules of 1951 inasmuch as the post of
A.D.O. has now been abolished. It is the prerogative
of the State to create or abolish a post. Admittedly,
the post of A.D.O. was an ex-cadre post, which has
now been abolished, but have protected the A.D.Os.
already working on these posts to continue, if they
so desire, till they retire or come back to their
original parent department willingly on their own
accord. Consequently, their claim that they should

19
be confirmed on the post of A.D.O., becomes
immaterial. The learned senior counsel submitted
that the third relief claimed has already been
granted, namely, that they are being paid the salary
of the post of a Deputy Ranger. Consequently, no
relief can be granted to the petitioners.
In so far as the petitioners of WPSS No.184 of
2006 are concerned, they are aggrieved by the order
of 6th June, 2005, by which they have been reverted
back to their parent department. These petitioners
were working as Foresters before they were deputed
to work as A.D.O.s. By the impugned order, the
petitioners will be reverted on the post of Foresters,
which is a lower post. The respondents admit that
the petitioner no.1 was working as an A.D.O. since
1995 and the petitioner nos.2 and 3 have been
working as A.D.O. since 2003. The respondents
admit that the post of A.D.O. is equivalent to the
post of Deputy Ranger and that the petitioners were
being paid the salary which was equivalent to the
post of Deputy Ranger. The respondents further
admit that if they are reverted back to the post of
Foresters, the petitioners would be given a lower
pay scale of the pay scale of a Forester and,
therefore, the petitioners would be put to a loss. In
this regard, the learned Additional Advocate
General submitted that to protect these A.D.O.s,
the Absorption Rules were framed.

20
Having heard the learned counsel for the
parties on this issue, the Court finds that even
though while deputing the petitioners as A.D.O.s, a
clear cut condition was imposed that persons will
not have any lien on the post of A.D.O. and they
could be reverted back at any moment of time when
regular A.D.O.s were appointed. It was also made
clear that the channel of promotion would be
governed by the Rules of the Forest Department of
the petitioners' parent department. But, having
said this, the action of the respondent becomes
arbitrary while reverting them to the parent
department on a lower post. The respondents could
send the petitioners back to the parent department,
but should ensure protection of their pay and the
post on which they are working. Since the post has
been abolished now, the petitioners can only be
adjusted on an equivalent post. The State as well as
all the petitioners in all the writ petitions admit
that the post of A.D.O. was equivalent to the post of
Deputy Ranger and, consequently, the Court is of
the opinion that the petitioners, if they have to be
sent back to the parent department, could only be
sent back on an equivalent post, which has the
same pay scale, so that the petitioners are not put
to any financial loss.
Consequently, the impugned order dated 6th
June, 2005, directing the petitioners to be reverted
back to their parent department on their original
post, cannot be sustained and is quashed. It is

21
clarified here that since the petitioners were
working for a considerable period of time on the
post of A.D.O., which carried a higher pay scale,
some right has accrued on them and, consequently,
on this short ground, they cannot be reverted back
to the post of Forester, i.e., their original posting.
In so far as the relief claimed by these
petitioners that they should be allowed to function
as A.D.O., such relief cannot be granted in the light
of the fact that the State Government has issued an
order dated 20th December, 2006, abolishing the
post of A.D.O., which is an ex-cadre post.
The third relief, namely, that the petitioners
should be promoted on the post of Forest Ranger,
under the direct recruitment, is based on the
submission of giving parity as given by the
Allahabad High Court with regard to the Junior
Forest Rangers. The petitioners have relied upon
the decision of the Allahabad High Court in the
case of Narendra Kumar Srivastava (Supra) and
contend that since the pay scale of Junior Forest
Ranger and A.D.O. was equivalent to Deputy
Ranger and such Junior Forest Rangers have been
given appointment as Forest Ranger by the State of
U.P., the petitioners should also be given similar
relief.
Having heard the learned counsel for the
petitioner on this point, the Court finds that such

22
relief cannot be granted. The question of parity
does not arise. The post of Junior Forest Ranger
may be equivalent to the post of Deputy Ranger and
the post of A.D.O. is also equivalent to the post of
Deputy Ranger, but the circumstances under which
the Junior Forest Rangers were appointed, were
totally different. Junior Forest Rangers were
appointed pursuant to an advertisement. There was
a condition stipulated in it that upon completion of
3 years of service as Junior Forest Rangers they
should be sent for training for a Rangers Course
and thereafter would be promoted, but were not
sent and, consequently, when an advertisement
was made in the year 1981 to fill up the post of
Forest Rangers, the Court issued an amendment
not to fill up some posts and directed the State
Government to fulfill their promissory obligations
made in the advertisement by amending the rules
and sending these Junior Forest Rangers for
training. Based on the said direction, Junior Forest
Rangers were eventually appointed as Forest
Rangers. The matter of Junior Forest Rangers is
totally different and distinguishable. The mere fact
that the pay scale of Junior Forest Rangers is
equivalent to the post of Deputy Ranger has no
relevance. The petitioners were not appointed on
the basis of any advertisement but were appointed
as Foresters under the Rules of 1951 and thereafter
were sent to work as A.D.O. upon options being
invited. The contention of the petitioners that they
were issued fresh appointment as A.D.O. is

23
misconceived and bereft of merit. The conditions of
appointment clearly indicated that their parent
cadre would be governed by the Rules of 1951 and
their channel of promotion would also be governed
by Service Rules, namely, the Rules of 1951. In the
light of the aforesaid, only a partial relief can be
granted to the petitioners of WPSS No.184 of 2006.
The contention of the State Government that
the petitioners have no locus standi to challenge
the promotion Rules of 2011, as they are not
affected by it, is misconceived. Even though, the
promotion Rules takes into consideration the
promotion of A.D.O.s in the direct recruitment
quota, nonetheless, the Court is of the opinion that
the petitioners are being affected by the fact that
persons who were originally working on the post of
Forest Guard or Forester would be promoted as
Forest Ranger and thereby will become senior to
the petitioners. The fact that by these Absorption
Rules, A.D.O.s would be promoted as Forest
Rangers in the direct recruitment quota, is
immaterial. What is material is that these A.D.O.s,
who were holding a lower post in the parent
department, would become senior by virtue of their
promotion on a higher post. The Court, accordingly
rejects the preliminary objection of the
respondents.
A perusal of the Absorption Rules of 2011
indicates that the same is applicable for absorption

24
on the post of Forest Range Officer against the
direct recruitment quota. These Rules also provide
that they shall have effect notwithstanding
anything to the contrary contained in any other
service rules made before. Rule 4(1) provides that
the appointing authority would issue orders for
absorption on the post of Forest Range Officer from
such persons posted against ex-cadre post of
Assistant Development Officer and that persons
who are appointed as Forest Range Officers would
be deemed to be appointed under the Service Rules
of 2010. The Absorption Rules of 2011 are
contradictory to the Service Rules of 2010 and
Entrance and Training Rules, 2004, which has
been framed under Rule 5(2) of the Rules of 1951.
The Court finds that under these Rules of 1951,
2010 and the Entrance and Training Rules 2004,
the basis rules of recruitment, educational
qualifications, age, physical fitness, recruitment
through Public Service Commission, written
examination, period of training have been given a
go-by, which in the opinion of the Court cannot be
done, being violative of Article 14 and 16 of the
Constitution. The basic rules of recruitment and
conditions of service as provided in the Service
Rules of 2010 framed under Article 309 cannot be
altered or changed by any other Rule. By this Rule,
a clear cut entry through back door method is
being provided for these A.D.O.s, who were initially
recruited as a Forest Guard or a Forester. The
channel of promotion from a Forest Guard to a

25
Forester to a Deputy Ranger and then to a Forest
Ranger cannot be bypassed by these Absorption
Rules, by simply saying that these Rules would
have an overriding effect to the earlier Rules. As a
result of these Absorption Rules, a Forester is
jumping one post, i.e., the post of Deputy Ranger
and is straightway being appointed as a Forest
Range Officer. A Forest Guard will jump two
promotions and would be absorbed as a Forest
Range Officer. Such Absorption Rules, in the
opinion of the Court, is per se arbitrary.
Article 14 provides equality to every person
before law and Article 16 provides equality of
opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to
appointment. These principles enshrined under
Article 14 and 16 are the guiding factors for making
Rules under Article 309 of the Constitution. The
basic principles enshrined under these two Articles
cannot be overlooked by making such haphazard
Rules under Article 309 of the Constitution.
The Court finds that under Rule 3(a) of the
Rules of 2010, the appointing authority for the post
of Forest Range Officer is the Principal Chief
Conservator of Forest. Under Rule 4(1) of the
Absorption Rules, 2011, the appointing authority is
required to absorb these A.D.O.s. The post of Forest
Range Officer is a gazetted post and is required to
be filled up by the Public Service Commission. By
virtue of these Absorption Rules of 2011, the Public

26
Service Commission is being bypassed. This is in
contradiction to the proviso to sub-clause (3) of
Article 320 of the Constitution of India, which
provides that regulations would be made specifying
the matters by which it shall not be necessary for
the Public Service Commission to be consulted,
meaning thereby, that if a post is within the
purview of a Public Service Commission, it can be
taken out of its purview provided such regulations
are framed. In the instant case, there is no such
order of the State Government excluding the post of
Forest Ranger from the purview of the Public
Service Commission. Infact, the State Government
in their counter affidavit, contends that the
Absorption Rules of 2011 has an overriding effect
on the constitutional provisions.
If a post is required to be filled up by a Public
Service Commission, the same cannot be bypassed.
The Public Service Commission is a constitutional
authority and cannot be bypassed in a manner
provided by the present Absorption Rules. It was
contended by the learned Additional Advocate
General that the Public Service Commission was
consulted and they opined that they have no
objection if such Absorption Rules are framed. The
stand of the respondent is patently erroneous in
this regard. If a post is required to be filled up by
recruitment through the Public Service
Commission, the State Government cannot direct
the appointing authority to consult the Public

27
Service Commission for absorption of their services,
in contradiction or in violation of the Statutory
Rules and Article 320 of the Constitution. The only
course available is to notify the recruitment to the
Public Service Commission and conduct the
examination inviting applications from all eligible
persons in accordance with the Rules.
In similar circumstances, in Union of India
vs. Others. vs. Harish Balkrishna Mahajan,
(1997) 3 Supreme Court Cases 194, the Supreme
Court held:
"3. The controversy is no longer res integra. In
similar circumstances, this Court had considered the
entire controversy in J&K Public Service Commission
v. Dr Narinder Mohan. Admittedly, the posts of
doctors in the Central Government Health Scheme
are required to be filled up by recruitment through
Union Public Service Commission. Therefore, the
direction to consider the case of the respondent in
consultation with the Public Service Commission for
regularization is in violation of the statutory rules
and Article 320 of the Constitution of India. The only
course known to law is that the Union of India shall
be required to notify the recruitment to the Public
Service Commission and the Union Public Service
Commission shall conduct the examination inviting
the applications from all the eligible persons
including the persons like the respondents. It would
be for the respondent to apply for and seek selection

28
in accordance with Rules. Therefore, the direction is
in violation of Article 320 of the Constitution."
In E. Ramakrishanan & Others vs. State of
Kerala and Others, (1996) 1 Supreme Court
Cases 565, the Supreme Court held that the State
Government cannot take any decision contrary to
the Constitution to regularize the services of the
candidate de hors the recruitment rules and
statutory process for selection from the Public
Service Commission.
Similarly, in P. Ravindran and Others vs.
Union Territory of Pondicherry and Others,
(1997) 1 Supreme Court Cases 350, the Supreme
Court held that where the Public Service
Commission has been entrusted with the
constitutional duties to select suitable candidates
by inviting candidates from the open market and
every candidate has a fundamental right to seek
consideration for selection through open
competition, such process cannot be bypassed by
issuing a direction for regularization of the services
of ad hoc persons who have come into service
through back door method.
In the light of the aforesaid, the Court finds
that there are existing Rules for recruitment on the
post of Forest Rangers by promotion and by way of
direct recruitment. Such procedure cannot be
bypassed by making Absorption Rules without

29
adhering to the qualification, written examination,
training, etc. nor the Public Service Commission
could be bypassed, which is a constitutional
authority. The process of selection as envisaged
under the Rules cannot be bypassed.
The Court, upon due consideration, finds that
the Absorption Rules of 2011 are not in conformity
with the Rules of 2004, which has been enacted by
the Government of India. The Absorption Rules of
2011 contravene various provisions of the Rules of
2004. Further, the Rules of 2011 is not in
conformity with the Rules of 2010, in which Rules
relating to recruitment and conditions of service
have been framed and such conditions of service
cannot be bypassed in the manner provided under
the Absorption Rules of 2011. The Court,
accordingly, finds that these Absorption Rules of
2011 are in violation of Article 14, 16 and 320 of
the Constitution of India and cannot be sustained
and are quashed.
Absorption as defined in the Concise Oxford
English Dictionary means the process of absorption
or the action of being absorbed.
In Kartar Singh & Others vs. State of Punjab
& Others, AIR (1990) Punjab and Haryana 1, the
Full Bench of the Punjab and Haryana High Court
held:

30
"40. Absorption thus has the effect of sucking
and imbibing in to what is originally existing. On
absorption thus an employee becomes part and
parcel of the department absorbing him and
partakes the same colour and character of the
existing employees of the department, classified as
promotees, direct appointees or transferees on the
loss of his identity..."
In the light of the aforesaid, absorption is no
doubt required to be done so that the persons who
were working on ad hoc post or on an ex-cadre post
can be absorbed in the parent department, but
such absorption can only be done on an equivalent
post. The respondents admit that the equivalent
post is that of a Deputy Ranger. If Absorption Rules
are required to be made, then the State
Government should absorb these A.D.O.s on the
post of Deputy Rangers, but by no stretch of
imagination, could an absorption be made on a
higher post, which has a different recruitment
procedure and which is on a higher pay scale. Such
Absorption Rules on the face of it, becomes
arbitrary.
In the light of the aforesaid, WPSS No.35/2012
and WPSS No.92/2012 are allowed and the
Absorption Rules of 2011 are quashed, being ultra
vires Article 14, 16 and 320 of the Constitution of
India.

31
WPSS No.292/2003, being devoid of merit, is
dismissed.
WPSS No.184/2006 is partly allowed. The
order dated 6th June, 2005 is quashed. The
petitioners in this writ petition are not entitled to
the other reliefs as claimed by them.
Before parting, it was stated by the Additional
Advocate General that there are only 10 A.D.O.s
working out of the original 76 posts and that their
demand for being absorbed in the parent cadre was
pending with the State Government for a long
period of time, on account of which, the impugned
Absorption Rules of 2011 were enacted. The post of
A.D.O. has been abolished in the year 2006 and,
consequently, these A.D.O.'s cannot be left in a
limbo and are required to be adjusted in the parent
department.
Considering all these aspects, the Court finds
that the State Government as well as the Principal
Chief Conservator of Forest admit that the ex-cadre
post of A.D.O. is equivalent to the post of Deputy
Ranger and, consequently, the Court directs that
these A.D.O.'s be adjusted on the post of Deputy
Ranger. The period spent by these A.D.O.s on the
post of Forest Guard or Forester and the period
spent on the post of A.D.O. will be calculated while
fixing their seniority on the post of Deputy Ranger
and a seniority list would be prepared accordingly.

32
The Court has been informed that the posts of
Forest Ranger are available in the Department. The
State Government, accordingly, should initiate the
exercise of filling up the post of Forest Ranger
under the relevant Rules of 2010 under the
promotion quota, as early as possible, through the
Public Service Commission, so that these A.D.O.'s
and other Deputy Rangers, who are eligible and
hold the essential qualifications, could apply and
be promoted.
In the light of the aforesaid, the Court directs
the State Government to do the needful in this
regard and initiate the process, as stated aforesaid,
within three months from the date of production of
a certified copy of the order and ensure that the
exercise of promotion is culminated and processed
through the Public Service Commission, as early as
possible, preferably within a period of six months
thereafter.
In the circumstances of the case, parties shall
bear their own cost.
